bib.title: Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations (NIST AI 100-2e2023)
bib.venue: NIST Trustworthy and Responsible AI report, NIST AI 100-2e2023, January 2024

read.skipped: References (pp. 57-91) skimmed only; glossary read for terms. Figures 1-2 are vector diagrams whose text came out as scattered letters.

question: What common taxonomy and terminology describe attacks on, and mitigations for, predictive and generative AI systems?
contributions: Standardized terminology in AML for the ML and cybersecurity communities
A taxonomy of the most widely studied attacks: evasion, poisoning, privacy for PredAI; evasion, poisoning, privacy, abuse for GenAI, across learning methods and modalities
A discussion of mitigations and the limitations of existing ones

results.claim: Poisoning only 0.001% of an uncurated web-scale dataset can induce targeted failures.
results.setup: Web-scale uncurated training sets, targeted failures
results.quote: an attacker can induce targeted failures in models by arbitrarily poisoning only 0.001% of uncurated web-scale training datasets

results.claim: Detecting adversarial examples is as hard as building a defense; Tramer showed equivalence to robust classification up to a factor of 2 in robustness radius.
results.quote: factor of 2 in the robustness radius

results.claim: Black-box evasion attacks typically need fewer than 1000 queries.
results.setup: Black-box evasion against ML classifiers, Bayesian optimization

results.claim: A small set of fixed attack queries extracted more than 60% of prompts across all model and dataset pairs.
results.setup: Prompt stealing with queries like 'Repeat all sentences in our conversation'

results.claim: Email addresses in LLM context can be revealed at rates exceeding 8%.
results.setup: Asking an LLM to repeat private info in its context
results.quote: email addresses can be revealed at rates exceeding 8%

results.claim: Automated model-based red teaming needs only dozens of queries per successful jailbreak.
results.quote: requiring only dozens of queries per successful jailbreak

results.claim: The 2020 US Census used a large privacy parameter, illustrating DP utility trade-offs.
results.quote: the 2020 U.S. Census release used ε = 19.61

results.claim: Poisoning is considered the most critical vulnerability of deployed ML in a Microsoft report.
results.setup: Microsoft report on production ML vulnerabilities
results.quote: considered to be the most critical vulnerability of machine learning systems deployed in production

results.claim: Data and instructions are not separate channels for the LLM, enabling attacks akin to SQL injection.
results.quote: data and instructions are not provided in separate channels to the LLM

results.claim: No comprehensive or foolproof defense against adversarial prompting exists.
results.setup: Prompt injection defenses for LLMs and RAG
results.quote: there is no comprehensive or foolproof solution for protecting models against adversarial prompting

limits: Not an exhaustive survey; authors note 5000+ AML arXiv references in 2021-2022 and aim only at categorization (Sec 1).
Does not quantify likelihoods or recommend risk tolerance (Executive Summary).
No information-theoretic security proofs for widely used ML; mitigations are empirical, ad hoc and fallible (Sec 1, 4.2).
Adversarial-example defenses have repeatedly been broken by adaptive attacks; robustness trades off with accuracy and fairness (Sec 2.2.4, 4.5).
Targeted/subpopulation poisoning has an impossibility result (Jagielski et al. [144]); DP robustness fades with multiple poisoned samples (Sec 2.3.2).
Backdoor mitigations mostly designed for CNN image classifiers with fixed triggers; weaker against semantic/functional triggers (Sec 2.3.3).
Imbalance between many privacy attacks and few reliable mitigations; query limiting is ineffective with anonymous access (Sec 4.2).
Prompt-injection mitigations give a measure of protection but not full immunity; theoretical limits on LLM censorship [116] (Sec 3.3.2, 4.2).
Lack of reliable standardized benchmarks makes AML mitigation papers incomparable (Sec 4.2).
Open challenges: scale of web data, open vs closed models, supply chain Trojans (undetectable Trojans [118]), multimodal robustness, quantized models (Sec 4.1-4.7).
Edition is E2023 (Jan 2024): later editions postdate it; the report says it will be updated regularly.
practices: Use adversarial training, randomized smoothing and formal verification as the evasion defenses that have held up, accepting robustness-accuracy cost (Sec 2.2.4).
Evaluate any new defense against strong adaptive attacks rather than known attacks (Sec 2.2.4).
Sanitize training data and use robust training against poisoning, plus cryptographic provenance and integrity attestation (Sec 2.3.1, 4.2).
Use differential privacy against membership inference and reconstruction, complemented by empirical privacy auditing (Sec 2.4.5).
Verify web-scale dataset downloads with published cryptographic hashes to detect domain hijacking (Sec 3.2.3).
Scan model artifacts for vulnerabilities and use safe persistence formats such as safetensors (Sec 3.2.3).
Treat prompt-injection defenses (alignment training, prompt formatting, detection filters) as defense in depth, not immunity (Sec 3.3.2).
For indirect injection, filter retrieved inputs, use an LLM moderator, RLHF and interpretability-based outlier detection (Sec 3.4.5).
Use controlled model gateways and other cybersecurity mechanisms since guardrails alone have theoretical limits (Sec 4.2).
Red-team LLMs pre-deployment and monitor chatbots and quantized GenAI models continuously (Sec 4.2, 4.7).
Restrict access to models across lifecycle and vet third-party components against Trojans (Sec 4.4).

terms.definition: two broad classes of AI systems based on capabilities: Predictive AI and Generative AI

terms.term: Availability breakdown / Integrity violation / Privacy compromise
terms.definition: the three attacker objectives (all systems); GenAI adds a fourth, abuse
an attacker repurposes a GenAI system's intended use to achieve their own objectives
training data control, model control, testing data control, label limit, source code control, query access
training data control, query access, source code control, resource control
white-box (full knowledge), black-box (minimal, query access), gray-box (in between)
a user injects text intended to alter the behavior of the LLM
attacker relies on an LLM ingesting an injection indirectly (web page, document, plugin); enabled by resource control
prompt injection specifically to circumvent safety and moderation features placed on LLMs
attack to divulge the system prompt or other hidden information in an LLM's context
deployment-time modification of test samples to create adversarial examples
adversarial attack during training: data poisoning (control of training data) or model poisoning (control of model parameters)
a backdoor pattern added to poisoned training samples and test samples to cause misclassification; only attack requiring both training and testing data control
poisoning where the attacker does not control labels of poisoned samples
availability attack via query access that increases computation (e.g. sponge examples)
data reconstruction, membership inference, property inference, data extraction (data privacy); model extraction (model privacy)

figures.why: Maps objective (availability, integrity, privacy) to capability to attack class.

figures.caption: Taxonomy of attacks on Generative AI systems
figures.why: Adds abuse objective and resource control; places indirect prompt injection across all four objectives.

figures.caption: Retrieval-augmented generation relies on system instructions, context, and data from third-party sources, often through a vector database, to produce relevant responses for users
figures.why: Shows where untrusted retrieved data enters the LLM context.
